steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Address remapping" section of the Wikipedia article on the 3 GB barrier: explain memory hole remapping on x86 chipsets, which Intel and AMD platforms support it, what it requires from the operating system, and how this affected MacBooks.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What memory remapping is and how the BIOS does it
- Support on Intel chipsets
- Support on AMD processors
- Operating system requirement (PAE)
- Effect on MacBooks

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What memory remapping is
  - x86 chipsets addressing more than 4 GiB of RAM usually allow it
  - some BIOS setup screens: "memory hole remapping"
  - BIOS detects address conflict, relocates interfering RAM to new physical address not conflicting with MMIO
- Intel
  - once limited to server chipsets
  - newer desktop chipsets: Intel 955X, 965 and later
  - "Memory Reclaiming" in chipset datasheet
- AMD
  - K8 and later: built-in memory controller had it from the beginning
- OS requirement
  - new physical addresses above 4 GiB -> OS must use physical addresses larger than 2^32
  - provided by PAE
  - OS need not support more than 4 GiB total; total RAM may be only 4 GiB, part of it just appears at addresses from 4 GiB up
- MacBooks
  - one generation affected, 1 year: Core2Duo (Merom), November 2006 to October 2007
  - prior generation: limited to 2 GiB
  - later (November 2007 – October 2009): 4 GiB via PAE + memory-hole remapping
  - late 2009 onwards: 64-bit processors, can address over 4 GiB

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
x86 chipsets that are able to address more than 4 GiB of RAM usually also allow memory remapping, which some BIOS setup screens call "memory hole remapping". With this, the BIOS detects the memory address conflict and relocates the RAM that interferes, so that the processor can address it at a new physical address which does not conflict with MMIO.

For Intel this feature used to be only in server chipsets, but newer desktop chipsets like the Intel 955X and 965 and later also have it (it is called "Memory Reclaiming" in the chipset datasheet).

For AMD, the built-in memory controller of the AMD K8 and later processors had it from the start.

- OS requirement
  - new physical addresses above 4 GiB -> OS must use physical addresses larger than 2^32
  - provided by PAE
  - OS need not support more than 4 GiB total; total RAM may be only 4 GiB, part of it just appears at addresses from 4 GiB up
- MacBooks
  - one generation affected, 1 year: Core2Duo (Merom), November 2006 to October 2007
  - prior generation: limited to 2 GiB
  - later (November 2007 – October 2009): 4 GiB via PAE + memory-hole remapping
  - late 2009 onwards: 64-bit processors, can address over 4 GiB

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
x86 chipsets that are able to address more than 4 GiB of RAM usually also allow memory remapping, which some BIOS setup screens call "memory hole remapping". With this, the BIOS detects the memory address conflict and relocates the RAM that interferes, so that the processor can address it at a new physical address which does not conflict with MMIO.

For Intel this feature used to be only in server chipsets, but newer desktop chipsets like the Intel 955X and 965 and later also have it (it is called "Memory Reclaiming" in the chipset datasheet).

For AMD, the built-in memory controller of the AMD K8 and later processors had it from the start.

The new physical addresses are above the 4 GiB point, so to address this RAM the operating system has to be able to use physical addresses larger than 2^32. PAE provides this capability. The operating system does not necessarily need to support more than 4 GiB of RAM in total, because the total RAM might only be 4 GiB, it is just that part of it shows up to the CPU at addresses from 4 GiB and up.

This form of the 3 GB barrier affects one generation of MacBooks, and it lasted 1 year (Core2Duo (Merom), November 2006 to October 2007). The generation before was limited to 2 GiB. Later generations (November 2007 – October 2009) allowed 4 GiB by using PAE and memory-hole remapping, and the generations after that (late 2009 onwards) use 64-bit processors so they can address over 4 GiB.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
x86 chipsets that can address more than 4 GiB of RAM typically also allow memory remapping (referred to in some BIOS setup screens as "memory hole remapping"). In this scheme, the BIOS detects the memory address conflict and in effect relocates the interfering RAM so that the processor can address it at a new physical address that does not conflict with MMIO.

On the Intel side, this feature was once limited to server chipsets; however, newer desktop chipsets such as the Intel 955X and 965 and later have it as well (see "Memory Reclaiming" in the chipset datasheet[1]).

On the AMD side, the built-in memory controller of the AMD K8 and later processors had it from the beginning.

As the new physical addresses are above the 4 GiB point, addressing this RAM requires that the operating system be able to use physical addresses larger than 2^32.[2] This capability is provided by PAE. Note that the operating system is not necessarily required to support more than 4 GiB of RAM in total, as the total RAM might be only 4 GiB; it is just that a portion of it appears to the CPU at addresses in the range from 4 GiB and up.[2]

This form of the 3 GB barrier affects one generation of MacBooks,[3] lasting 1 year (Core2Duo (Merom) – November 2006 to October 2007): the prior generation was limited to 2 GiB, while later generations (November 2007 – October 2009) allowed 4 GiB by using PAE and memory-hole remapping, and subsequent generations (late 2009 onwards) use 64-bit processors and can therefore address over 4 GiB.

References:
[1] (July 2006). Intel 965 Express Chipset Family. Intel. https://www.intel.com/Assets/PDF/datasheet/313053.pdf
[2] Intel Corporation. (February 2005). Intel Chipset 4 GB System Memory Support. Pentium Pro Family Developer's Manual. http://dlsvr01.asus.com/pub/ASUS/mb/4GB_Rev1.pdf
[3] Understanding Intel Mac RAM. http://guides.macrumors.com/Understanding_Intel_Mac_RAM
